words: From re- + act. Piecewise doublet of redact.
From Middle English relaxen, from Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre (“relax, loosen, open”), from re- (“back”) + laxāre (“loosen”)
To make (something) new again; to restore to freshness or original condition.
From Middle English renewen, an alteration (possibly on analogy with Latin renovāre) of earlier anewen (“to renew”), from Old English nīewian (“to restore; renovate; renew”), equivalent to re- + new.
To set back to the initial state.
The act of salvaging or in some manner restoring a discarded item to yield something usable.
To withdraw, retract (one's words etc.); to revoke (an order).
From re- + call, probably modelled on Latin revocāre, French rappeler, English withcall.
An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.
From Middle English recorde, borrowed from Old French record, from recorder. See record.
To bring down the size, quantity, quality, value or intensity of something; to diminish, to lower.
From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”). See duke, and compare with redoubt.
To purify; reduce to a fine, unmixed, or pure state; to free from impurities.
An automatic response to a simple stimulus which does not require mental processing.
From Late Latin reflexus, past participle of reflectere (“to bend back”), equivalent to re- + flex. Photography sense is from noun sense meaning “reflection”.
From Middle English refunden, refounden, from Old French refondre, refonder, refunder (“to restore; pay back”)
Borrowed into late Middle English from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (“to refuse”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (“to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding…
To get back; to recover possession of.
From Middle French regaigner (French regagner). By surface analysis, re- + gain.
To feel sorry about (a thing that has or has not happened), afterthink: to wish that a thing had not happened, that something else had happened instead.
From Middle English regretten, regreten, from Old French regreter, regrater (“to lament”), from re- (intensive prefix) + *greter, *grater (“to weep”), from Frankish *grātan (“to weep, mourn, lament”)
To refuse to accept; to forswear.
From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”)
An act of pointing out or noticing; notice or observation.
From Middle French remarquer, from Old French remarquer, from re- (“again”) + marquer (“to mark”), equivalent to re- (“again”) + mark.
From Middle English remedie, from Old French *remedie, remede, from Latin remedium (“a remedy, cure”), from re- (“again”) + mederi (“to heal”).
To cause one to experience a memory (of someone or something); to bring to the notice or consideration (of a person).
From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind (“to remember”). Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate with the same sense. Displaced Old English myndgian.
From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote, feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (“to remove”), from re- + movere (“to move”).
From Middle English removen, from Anglo-Norman remover, removeir, from Old French remouvoir, from Latin removēre.
To reverse the effects of an action.
From Middle English undōn, from Old English ondōn.
Not set; not fixed or appointed.
Not able; lacking a certain ability.
From Middle English unable, unabel, unhable, unhabil, equivalent to un- + able.
Undeservedly; in a way that is not warranted.
From Middle English unesy, equivalent to un- + easy. Merged with Middle English unethe, uneathe (“difficult, not easy”). See uneath.
From Middle English unfair (“unattractive, unseemly”), from Old English unfæġer (“ugly”), equivalent to un- + fair.
Not like; dissimilar (to); having no resemblance; unalike.
From Middle English unlic, unlich, from Old English unlīċ, unġelīċ (“unlike, different, dissimilar, diverse”)
To remove the load or cargo from (a vehicle, etc.).
To undo or open a lock or something locked by, for example, turning a key, or selecting a combination.
From Middle English unloken, unlouken, onlouken, from Old English onlūcan (“to unlock”), equivalent to un- + lock.
From Middle English unsen, unseyn, unseien, from Old English unġesewen.
From Middle English unsure, equivalent to un- + sure. Piecewise doublet of insecure and unsecure.
From Middle English untrewe, from Old English untrīewe.
From Middle English unwis, from Old English unwīs (“unwise, foolish, ignorant, uninformed, insane”), equivalent to un- + wise.
Not aware or informed; lacking knowledge; unmindful.
Ambiguous; liable to more than one interpretation.
From Middle English unclere, equivalent to un- + clear.
Worthy of note; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished.
Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”)
That can be argued; that can be proven or strongly supported with sound logical deduction, precedent, and evidence.
Able to be carried or easily moved.
From Middle English portable, from Middle French portable and Latin portābilis. By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -able.
Legible, possible to read or at least decipher.
Inherited from Middle English redable. By surface analysis, read + -able.
Suitable or fit to be relied on; dependable, trustworthy
Having sufficient or the required properties for a certain purpose or task; appropriate to a certain occasion.
Able to vary or be varied.
Borrowed into Middle English in the 14th century from Old French variable, from Latin variare (“to change”), from varius (“different, various”). Equates to English vary + -able.
From Middle English admyrable, partly from Middle French admirable and partly from its etymon, Latin admirābilis. By surface analysis, admire + -able.
From Middle English allowable, alowable, a borrowing from Old French alouable (Modern French allouable), from allouer, equivalent to allow + -able.
Such as one may avail oneself of; capable of being used for the accomplishment of a purpose.
From Middle English available, avayllable, avayleable, equivalent of avail + -able.
Open to debate; not fully proved or confirmed.
From Old French debatable (French débattable), equivalent to debate + -able.
Worthy to be desired; pleasing; agreeable.
Worthy to be remembered; very important or remarkable.
From Middle English memorable, memorrable, from Latin memorābilis, from memorō (“to bring to remembrance”), from memor (“mindful, remembering”). By surface analysis, memory + -able, see memory.
In a state of misery: very sad, ill, or poor.
Borrowed from Middle French miserable, from Old French, from Latin miserabilis, equivalent to miser + -able.
Capable, worthy, or sure of being accepted or received with pleasure; welcome; gratifying; pleasing to a receiver.
From Middle English acceptable, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French acceptable, from Late Latin acceptābilis (“worthy of acceptance”).
From Middle English bilevable, beleevable, equivalent to believe + -able.
To render unable; to take away an ability of, as by crippling.
To cause an intense dislike for something.
Borrowed from Middle French desgouster, from Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”)
An attitude or a feeling of distaste or aversion.
To discharge; to end the employment or service of.
To throw into confusion or disorder.
Borrowed from Latin disruptus, from disrumpo, commonly dirumpo (“to break or burst asunder”), from dis-, di- (“apart, asunder”) + rumpo (“to break”).
Made incapable of use or action.
To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.
From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”)
An unfortunate or unpleasant occurrence, especially one resulting from an accident or something going wrong.
From Middle French desastre, from Italian disastro, from dis- + astro (“star”), from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”)
To sell at a reduced price.
To find or learn something for the first time.
From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Displaced native Old English onfindan.
From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”).
Material (such as clothing, makeup, a wig) used to alter one’s visual appearance in order to hide one's identity or assume another.
From Middle English disgisen, disguisen, borrowed from Old French desguiser (modern French déguiser), itself derived from des- (“dis-”) (from Latin dis-) + guise (“guise”) (from a Germanic source).
Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.
Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō).
An amount of space between points (often geographical points), usually (but not necessarily) measured along a straight line.
From Middle English distance, distaunce, destance (“disagreement, dispute; discrimination; armed conflict; hostility; trouble; space between two points; time interval”)
Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).
Physical or emotional discomfort, suffering, or alarm, particularly of a more acute nature.
The verb is from Middle English distressen.
An administrative division of an area.
From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”)
From Middle English disapeeren, equivalent to dis- + appear. Displaced native Old English fordwīnan.
To accomplish or complete, as an obligation.
From Middle English dischargen, from Old French deschargier (“to unload”), from Late Latin discarricāre (“unload”). By surface analysis, dis- + charge.
From Middle English agheful, awfull, auful, aȝefull, equivalent to awe + -ful.
From Middle English synful, senful, sunful, from Old English synful (“sinful, guilty, wicked, corrupt”), equivalent to sin + -ful.
Having a practical or beneficial use.
Attentive to potential danger, error or harm; cautious.
From Middle English careful, from Old English carful; equivalent to care + -ful.
A small number, usually approximately five.
From Middle English handful, hondful, from Old English handfull (“handful”)
From Middle English harmful, from Old English *hearmful (suggested by hearmfullīċ (“harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to harm + -ful.
From Middle English helpful; equivalent to help + -ful.
Someone who is hoping for success or victory, especially as a candidate in a political election.
Requiring effort or labor; difficult, laborious.
From Middle English paynful, peinful, peynful, paynefull, peynefull, equivalent to pain + -ful.
From Middle English chereful, cherful, equivalent to cheer + -ful.
From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.
A shocker: a report of a crime written in a provokingly lurid style.
From Middle English dredful, dredfull, dredeful (also dreful). By surface analysis, dread + -ful.
Loyal; adhering firmly to person or cause.
From Middle English feithful, equivalent to faith + -ful.
Of a person or their actions, feelings, etc.: expressing gratitude or appreciation; appreciative, thankful.
From grate (“(obsolete) serving to gratify, agreeable, pleasing; grateful, thankful”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives with the sense of tending to have or thoroughly having a quality). Grate is…
Not at war; not disturbed by strife or turmoil.
From Middle English peesful, pesful, paisful, pesefull. By surface analysis, peace + -ful. Displaced native Old English friþsum.
Leading to many or important deductions.
From Middle English pouerful, powarfull. By surface analysis, power + -ful.
From Middle English thankful, from Old English þancful, þancfull (“thoughtful, pleasing, agreeable, pleasant, thankful, grateful”), equivalent to thank + -ful.
Possessing beauty, impressing the eye; attractive.
From Middle English bewteful, beautefull (“attractive to the eye, beautiful”), equivalent to beauty + -ful. In this sense, largely displaced Old English fæġer (whence fair).
From Middle English wonderful, wondirful, from Old English wundorful (“wonderful”)
Pleasant; pleasing, bringing enjoyment, satisfaction, or pleasure.
From Middle English deliteful, delitfull, equivalent to delight + -ful.
From Middle English endeles, from Old English endelēas (“endless”)
Without use or the possibility to be used.
From Middle English careles, from Old English carlēas (“careless, reckless, void of care, free from care, free”), equivalent to care + -less.
Incapable of causing harm or danger; safe.
From Middle English harmles, from Old English *hearmlēas.
From Middle English helples, from Old English *helplēas (“helpless”)
Without hope; despairing; not expecting anything positive.
Showing a lack of forethought or sense.
From Middle English myndles, myndelees, myndeles, mendlees, from Old English myndlēas, ġemyndlēas (“foolish, senseless”), equivalent to mind + -less.
From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less.
From Middle English needlees, nedelees, nedeles, equivalent to need + -less.
Free from pain; without pain or trouble.
From Middle English paynles, peynlees, equivalent to pain + -less.
Careless or heedless; headstrong or rash.
From Middle English rekles, reckeles, rekkeles, (also recheles), from Old English rēcelēas (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to reck + -less.
having no tact; unaware or intentionally inconsiderate of someone else's feelings
A huge and uncountable number of; too many to count; innumerable.
Characterized by or experiencing no doubt at all, certain; undoubted; undoubting.
From Middle English douteles, dowteles, equivalent to doubt + -less.
Having no point or sharp tip; terminating squarely or in a rounded end.
From Middle English pointles, poynteles, poyntlees. By surface analysis, point + -less.
Having no worth or use; without value.
From Middle English *worthles, from Old English weorþlēas (“worthless”), equivalent to worth + -less.
In a manner showing no hope.
Without attention to warnings or indications of bad consequences.
An instance (episode) of a disease or poor health.
The state of being mad; insanity; mental disease.
From Middle English madnes, madnesse; equivalent to mad + -ness.
The state of being dark; lack of light; the absolute or comparative absence of light.
From Middle English derknesse, from Old English deorcnes; equivalent to dark + -ness.
The property of being fair or equitable.
From Middle English fairness, fæȝernesse, from Old English fæġernes (“fairness; beauty; pleasantness”), equivalent to fair + -ness.
The state or characteristic of being good.
From Middle English goodnesse, godnesse, from Old English gōdnes (“goodness; virtue; kindness”)
From Middle English kyndenesse, equivalent to kind + -ness.
From Middle English weyknesse, replacing earlier Middle English wocnesse, wakenes, wacnesse (“weakness”), from Old English wācnes (“weakness”). Equivalent to weak + -ness.
The state or level of consciousness where sense data can be confirmed by an observer.
The emotion of being happy; joy; elation.
The property of being thick (in dimension).
From Middle English thikkenesse, thiknesse, from Old English þicnes (“thickness, viscosity, density, hardness; obscurity, cloud, darkness; thicket; depth, a thick body, anything thick or heavy”)
From Middle English bryghtnes, brightnesse, from Old English beorhtnes (“brightness, splendor”)
The quality or degree of being useful.
The state or quality of being serious.
The state or condition of being complete.
The state of being conscious or aware; awareness.
The property of being effective, of achieving results.
Suitability; the quality of being apt or suitable.
The quality or degree of being bad.
From Middle English baddenes, badnes, badnesse; equivalent to bad + -ness.
Late; especially, past a deadline or too late to fulfill a need.
To co-occur, to happen at the same time.
To surmount (a physical or abstract obstacle); to prevail over, to get the better of.
Inherited from Middle English overcomen, inherited from Old English ofercuman (“to overcome, subdue, compel, conquer, obtain, attain, reach, overtake”). By surface analysis, over- + come.
An outlet for escape of excess material.
From Middle English overflowen, from Old English oferflōwan, equivalent to over- + flow.
Located above, especially over the head.
From Middle English owerheved, over-hed, over hede (adverb), from Old English oferhēafod (adverb), equivalent to over- + head.
A vista or point that gives a view down toward something else.
To ride across or beyond something.
From Middle English overriden, from Old English oferrīdan, equivalent to over- + ride.
Working time outside of one's regular hours.
An implicit message (in a film, book, verbal discussion, or similar) perceived as overwhelming the explicit message.
From over- + tone, calque of German Oberton.
A brief summary, as of a book or a presentation.
To extract groundwater from (an aquifer) beyond the safe yield or equilibrium yield.
to give a commodity an excessive price
To engulf, surge over and submerge.
Inherited from Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.
To do too much; to exceed what is proper or true in doing; to carry too far.
From Middle English overdon, from Old English oferdōn, equivalent to over- + do.
To act in an exaggerated manner.
Borrowed from Late Latin praefīxum, from Latin praefīxus, past participle of praefīgō (“to (fix, fasten, set up) in front”, “to fix on the (end, extremity)”) (from prae- (“before”) + fīgō (“to…
To go before, go in front of.
From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.
To prophesy a future event on the basis of mystical knowledge or power.
An introduction, or series of preliminary remarks.
To make ready for a specific future purpose; to set up; to assemble or equip; to forearm.
To assume or suggest to be true (without proof); to take for granted, to suppose.
From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).
To speak or behave so as to give a false or simulated appearance.
From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”)
An experience of something in advance.
From pre- + view; compare Old French preveü, past participle of preveoir (“to foresee”).
An adverse judgment or opinion formed beforehand or without knowledge of the facts.
From Middle English prejudice, from Old French prejudice, derived from Latin praeiūdicium (“previous judgment or damage”), from prae- (“before”) + iūdicium (“judgment”).
Occurring before a state of readiness or maturity has arrived.
From Latin praemātūrus, equivalent to pre- + mature. First use appears c. 1440 in a translation of Palladius's De Re Rustica.
To specify by writing as a required procedure or ritual; to lay down authoritatively as a guide, direction, or rule of action.
Borrowed from Latin praescrībere, from prae- (“before, in front”) and scrībere (“to write”).
From Latin praevalēns. By surface analysis, pre- + -valent.
A person who sees a film or TV program, etc. before its general release to the public.
Previous caution or care; caution previously employed to prevent misfortune or to secure good.
From French précaution, Latin praecautio, from praecavere, praecautum (“to guard against beforehand”); prae (“before”) + cavere (“be on one's guard”). See pre-, and caution.
One who precedes; one who has preceded another in any state, position, office, etc.; one whom another follows or comes after, in any office or position.
From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”)
In preparation for the main matter; initial, introductory, preparatory.
Borrowed from New Latin praelīmināris, formed from prae- (“before”) + līmen (“threshold”) + -āris (adjectival suffix); compare Latin līmināris (“of or belonging to a threshold”).
Required as a prior condition of something else; necessary or indispensable.
Any plan of treatment or handling; the treatment or handling thus provided.
Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French prescripcion, from Latin praescriptio (“preface; pretext; something written ahead of time”)
To pay in advance, or beforehand
Set in advance, especially as a default.

meaning: Bad or wrong; badly or wrongly.
words: An incorrect, improper or unlawful use of something.
To lead astray, in a false direction.
From Middle English mysleden, from Old English mislǣdan (“to mislead”)
To read wrongly; misconstrue; misinterpret; mistake the sense or significance of.
From Middle English misreden, from Old English misrǣdan (“to advise wrongly; read wrongly”), equivalent to mis- + read.
To understand wrongly, taking one thing or person for another.
From Middle English mistaken, from Old Norse mistaka (“to take in error, to miscarry”); equivalent to mis- + take.
To guide poorly or incorrectly; to lead astray or into error.
To put something somewhere and then forget its location; to mislay.
Of a person: lacking proper guidance; misled or mistaken in one's actions or thinking.
From misguide + -ed (suffix forming adjectives; and past tense and past participle forms of regular verbs).
An instance of bad luck, an undesirable event such as an accident.
To make an incorrect interpretation; to misunderstand.
To represent falsely; to inaccurately portray something.
To understand incorrectly, while believing one has understood correctly.
From Middle English mys-understanden, equivalent to mis- + understand.
From Middle English misdon, from Old English misdōn (“to do evil, transgress, do amiss, err”)
A miss of the object one intended to hit.
A failure to fit well; unsuitability, disparity.
From Middle English mishap, myshappe, myssehappe, equivalent to mis- + hap.
To leave or lay something in the wrong place and then forget where one put it.
From Middle English mysse layen, equivalent to mis- + lay.
To call (someone or something) incorrectly or by the wrong title or name.
From Middle English miscallen, equivalent to mis- + call.
From Middle English miscasten, equivalent to mis- + cast.

meaning: A branch of learning; a study of a particular subject.
words: The study of all life or living matter.
Borrowed from New Latin biologia (1766), itself from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”). By surface analysis, bio- + -logy.
Any study of the relationships of components of a system with their environment and with each other.
Calque of German Ökologie (coined in 1866 by Ernst Haeckel), from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + -λογία (-logía, “study of”). By surface analysis, eco- + -logy.
The science that studies the structure of the Earth (or other planets), together with its origin and development, especially by examination of its rocks.
From geo- + -logy, partly after Renaissance Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-, “earth”) + Latin -logia (“the study of”), from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).
Doctrine, philosophy, body of beliefs or principles belonging to an individual or group.
Borrowed from French idéologie, from idéo- + -logie (equivalent to English ideo- + -logy).
The study of God, a god, or gods; and of the truthfulness of religion in general.
From Middle English theologie, from Middle French theologie, from Old French theologie, from Latin theologia, from Koine Greek θεολογία (theología), from θεολόγος (theológos, adjective)
The study of the physical universe, its structure, dynamics, origin and evolution, and fate.
From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”). By…
The entire catalogue of meanings that a word, morpheme, or sign has carried throughout its history.
From Middle English ethymologie, from Old French ethimologie, from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología)
The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
A branch of biology that deals with the functions and activities of life or of living matter (as organs, tissues, or cells) and of the physical and chemical phenomena involved.
From French physiologie, from Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología, “natural philosophy”)
The combined application of science and art in practical ways in industry, as for example in designing new machines.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología, “systematic treatment (of grammar)”), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”) + -λογία (-logía, “study”). By surface analysis, techno- + -logy.
A treatise on terms, especially those used in a specialised field.
From French terminologie or German Terminologie and their source, New Latin terminologia, from Medieval Latin terminus (“a term”) + -ologia (“study of”)
The surgical specialty of medicine that treats disorders of the urinary tract and the urogenital system.
From Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + λόγος (lógos, “knowledge”). By surface analysis, zoo- + -logy. Piecewise doublet of biology.
The study or measurement of time
From Latin horologia, from horo- + -logia, equivalent to Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “period of time, hour”) + -λογία (-logía, “-ology: study or proper knowledge of”). Equivalent to horo- + -ology.
The branch of medicine concerned with tumors, including study of their development, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.
Any collection τ of subsets of a given set X that contains both the empty set and X, and which is closed under finitary intersections and arbitrary unions.
From Late Latin topologia, from By surface analysis, topo- (“place”) + -logy (“study of, a branch of knowledge”).
The branch of microbiology that deals with the study of viruses and viral diseases.
Divination about human affairs or natural phenomena from the relative positions of celestial bodies.
From Middle French astrologie, and its source, Latin astrologia (“astronomy”), from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “telling of the stars”)
The branch of anthropology that compares and analyzes different human cultures and the relationships between them.
To experience; to pass through a phase.
From Middle English undergon, from Old English undergān (“to undergo, undermine, ruin”), equivalent to under- + go.
To provide a support for something
From Middle English underleyen, from Old English underleċġan (“to underlay, prop, support”), equivalent to under- + lay.
To lie in a position directly beneath something.
From Middle English underlien, underliggen, from Old English underliċġan (“to underlie, to be subject to, give way to”), equivalent to under- + lie.
A line placed underneath a piece of text in order to provide emphasis or to indicate that it should be viewed in italics or (in electronic documents) that it acts as a hyperlink.
To take upon oneself; to start, to embark on.
From Middle English undertaken; equivalent to under- + take (after undernim).
From Middle English undernethe, undernethen, from Old English underneoþan (“underneath”), ultimately.
To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.
From Middle English understanden, from Old English understandan (“to understand”)
Below the ground; below the surface of the Earth.
From Middle English undergrounde (adverb), equivalent to under + ground or under- + ground.
A lining on the inside of a garment.
To estimate too low; to perceive (someone or something) as having a lower value, quantity, worth, etc., than what he/she/it actually has.
A student at a university who has not yet received a degree.
Below the legal age (usually age 18 or 21) for some activity, such as consuming alcohol or engaging in sexual intercourse.
From under- + arm. The armpit sense is not old, historically speaking (1920s), and it is believed to have arisen as a euphemism in advertising.
A cut made in the lower part of something; the material so removed.
From Middle English undercutten, equivalent to under- + cut.
A competitor thought unlikely to win.
To pay (someone) less than the value of their work; to pay (someone) insufficiently.
To support from below with props or masonry.
Existing, relating to, or made for use beneath the sea, that is, beneath the sea surface, inside the sea.

meaning: A position which is in between two (or more) of the kind indicated by the root.
words: The point of interconnection or contact between entities.
To disturb or halt (an ongoing process or action, or the person performing it) by interfering suddenly, especially by speaking.
From Middle English interrupten, derived from Latin interruptus, past participle of interrumpere (“to break apart/off, interrupt”), from inter (“between”) + rumpere (“to break”).
Any face-to-face meeting, especially of an official or adversarial nature.
From Old French entreveue (French entrevue), feminine singular past participle of entrevëoir, from entre- + vëoir (“to see”). Equivalent to inter- + view.
Influencing or having an effect on each other; acting or capable of acting on each other or with the other.
Stopping and starting, occurring, or presenting at intervals; coming after a particular time span.
From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).
Of or having to do with more than one nation.
From inter- + national. Introduced in modern English by Jeremy Bentham in his An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1780.
The noun is a variant of Internet. The verb is derived from the noun.
To plead on someone else's behalf.
From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”)
From Middle English entrelacen, from Anglo-Norman entrelacer, from Old French inter- + lacer (“weave”).
To fit or clasp together securely.
To cut into or between; to cut or cross mutually; to divide into parts.
From Latin intersecare (“to cut between, cut off”), from inter (“between”) + secare (“to cut”).
To breed or reproduce within an isolated community.
To insert (pages, which are normally blank) between the pages of a book.
One who interferes, intrudes, or gets involved where not welcome; particularly, a self-interested intruder.
From inter- + loper (“runner, rover”), as in landloper (“vagrant”) (from lope (“to leap, to jump”) (originally dialectal)). Originally spelt enterloper and used in specific sense, “unauthorized…
A group of things or people, all of which are in a specified larger group.
An underground railway, especially for mass transit of people in urban areas.
To write (one’s name) at the bottom of a document; to sign (one's name).
From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere (“write beneath”). By surface analysis, sub- + scribe.
The act of submitting or yielding; surrender.
From Middle English submissioun, from Old French soubmission, from Latin submissio, from submitto.
A section of code, called by the main body of a program, that implements a task.
To use in place of something else, with the same function.
From Middle English substituten, from Latin substitutus, past participle of substituō.
Access to a resource for a period of time, generally for payment.
From Latin subscriptiō; by surface analysis, sub- + script + -ion. All senses reflect (either literally or figuratively) the notion of signing one's own name beneath some promise or description to…
From Old French suburbe, subburbe, from Latin suburbium (from sub- (“under-”) + urbs (“city”)). Displaced native Old English underburg (literally “underborough”).
To add something to the end; to append or annex.
To raise (someone or an intangible thing) to a state of (especially moral or spiritual) excellence; to exalt.
A plot within a story, subsidiary to the main plot.
Financial support or assistance, such as a grant.
From Middle English subsidy, subsidie, from Anglo-Norman subsidee, subsidie, from Old French subside, from Latin subsidium (support, assistance), from subsido from sub- (“below”) + sīdō (“sit”).
The layer of earth that is below the topsoil.
To place (any one cognition) under another as belonging to it; to include or contain something else.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin subsūmere, from sub- + sūmō (“to take”).
Below the age of a teenager, younger than thirteen years old.
A secondary class within a main class.
A group within a larger group; a group whose members are some, but not all, of the members of a larger group.
Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.
In which the value of a data item (such as time) is represented by a continuous(ly) variable physical quantity that can be measured (such as the shadow of a sundial).
A word or phrase that is created by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase.
A relationship of resemblance or equivalence between two situations, people, or objects, especially when used as a basis for explanation or extrapolation.
From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).
The science that deals with the form and structure of organic bodies
From Middle English anatomie, from Old French anatomie, from Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”, literally “cutting up”)
An organ or structure that is similar in function to one in another kind of organism but is of dissimilar evolutionary origin.
Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -logue. See analog.
Decomposition into components in order to study (a complex thing, concept, theory, etc.).
From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis), from ἀναλύω (analúō, “to unravel, investigate”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “thoroughly”) + λύω (lúō, “to loosen”).
Of or relating to anatomy or dissection.
From anatomic + -al, after -ical. By surface analysis, anatomy + -ical.
A chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object.
From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”)
Erroneous in date; in a wrong time; not applicable to or not appropriate for the time.
To replace or enhance human labor with machines.
Capable of operating without external control or intervention.
Borrowed from New Latin automaticus, from Classical Latin automatum (“automaton”) + -icus (adjectival suffix)
From French automobile, from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autós, “self”) + French mobile (“moving”), from Latin mōbilis (“movable”), equivalent to auto- (“self”) + mobile.
A self-written biography; the story of one's own life.
An absolute ruler with infinite power.
Borrowed from French autocrate, itself from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”)
The right or condition of self-government; freedom to act or function independently.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek αὐτονομῐ́ᾱ (autonomĭ́ā, “freedom to use its own laws, independence”)
A form of government in which unlimited power is held by a single individual.
From auto- + -cracy, from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατία (autokratía, “A system of government by one person with absolute power.”)
A person’s own handwriting, especially the signature of a famous or admired person.
From Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). Equivalent to auto- + -graph.
A state of mind where one no longer thinks about doing one's actions, but acts mechanically.
Absolute; holding independent and arbitrary powers of government.
Having the ability to move by itself; self-propelled or self-propelling.
Of or relating to a person's life or an account of a person's life, as told by the subject.
Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse.
From Middle English contrarie, compare French contraire, from Old French contraire, from Latin contrārius (“opposite, opposed, contrary”), from contrā (“against”).
A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable.
From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).
To deny the truth or validity of (a statement or statements).
Derived from Latin contrādictus (“contradicted”), the past participle of contrādīcō (“speak against”) (originally two words).
The chief accounting officer which audits, and manages the financial affairs of a company or government; a comptroller.
From Middle English countreroller, from Anglo-Norman contreroulour and Middle French contreroleur (French contrôleur), from Medieval Latin contrārotulātor, from *contrārotulāre (from which control).
A debate or discussion of opposing opinions; (generally) strife.
From Middle English controversie, from Old French controversie, from Latin contrōversia (“debate, contention, controversy”), from contrōversus (“turned in an opposite direction”).
A logical inconsistency among two or more elements or propositions.
From Middle English contradiccioun, contradiction, from Old French contradiction, from Latin contrādictiō, from contrādīcō (“speak against”).
Distinction by contrast; the provision of one example against which another example may be defined.
A plan, drawing, sketch or outline to show the function or operation of something, or to show the relationships between the parts of a whole.
From French diagramme, from Italian diagramma, from Ancient Greek διάγραμμα (diágramma).
A variant of a non-standardized programming language.
From Middle French dialecte, from Latin dialectos, dialectus.
A conversation or other form of discourse between two or more individuals.
Inherited from Middle English dialog, from Old French dialoge (French dialogue), from Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos, “conversation, discourse”)
Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a chord that passes through the center of the circle.
From Old French diametre (French diamètre), from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros) (γραμμή (grammḗ)) (diametros grammē, “line measuring across”)
The process of, or an instance of, identification of the nature and cause of something (of any nature).
From Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis), from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to discern”), from διά (diá, “through”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to know”).
Serving to indicate or specify a particular item or thing within a group of similar things.
From Ancient Greek διαγνωστικός (diagnōstikós), adjective from διαγιγνώσκω (diagignṓskō, “to distinguish, diagnose”).
To determine the cause of a problem.
The spelling out of alternatives, or presenting of either-or arguments that lead to a conclusion.
From Latin dialysis, from Ancient Greek διάλυσις (diálusis). By surface analysis, dia- + -lysis. First use appears c. 1550.
An abusive, bitter verbal or written attack, criticism or denunciation.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek διακριτικός (diakritikós, “distinguishing, separative”), from διακρῑ́νω (diakrī́nō, “to distinguish, separate”)
Peculiar to a (nonstandard) variety or lect.
Transparent or translucent; allowing light to pass through; capable of being seen through.
From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).
Capable of distinguishing or of making a distinction.
In the form of a diagram.
A person who diagnoses, especially a medical doctor.

meaning: External to, on the outside of
words: From Middle English outcry, outcri, outcrye, equivalent to out- + cry.
An onset; the beginning or initial stage of something.
From out- + set, replacing earlier outsetting.
A place from which something can be viewed.
To exceed in weight or mass.
From outstand, equivalent to out- + standing or outstand + -ing.
To excel; go beyond in performance; surpass.
The act or process of going out; (countable) an instance of this
The verb is derived from Middle English outgon (“to go out, depart, leave; to come out, emerge; to escape; to protrude; of a sword: to be drawn; to emanate from (a place); to accompany”)
To bid more than (somebody else) in an auction.
To beat (someone) in a competition of wits with superior cleverness or cunning; to outsmart.
From Middle English outlawe, outlagh, utlaȝe, from Old English ūtlaga (“outlaw”), borrowed from Old Norse útlagi (“outlaw, fugitive”), equivalent to out- + law.
A laying out or expending; that which is laid out or expended.
A vent or similar passage to allow the escape of something.
From Middle English outlete, outeleate, ut-lete, derived from Middle English outleten (“to allow, let out, emit”), equivalent to out- + let.
To get the better of; to outsmart, to beat in a competition of wits.
From Middle English outcasten, equivalent to out- + cast.
A piece of land that stands out (usually into water) from the land surrounding.
Situated in, designed to be used in, or carried on in the open air.
To become too big in size or too mature in age or outlook to continue to want, need, use, experience, or accept some object, practice, condition, belief, etc.
To live, last or remain longer than.
From Middle French social, from Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion or companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, fellow, partner, associate, ally”)
A long-standing group of people sharing cultural aspects such as language, dress, norms of behavior and artistic forms.
Borrowed from Middle French societé, from Old French societé, from Latin societās, societātem (“fellowship, association, alliance, union, community”)
Joined with another or others and having lower status.
From Middle English associat(e) (used participially as well as adjectively up to Early Modern English), from Latin associātus, the perfect passive participle of associō (“to join, unite”)
Unwilling or unable to cooperate and associate normally with other people.
A connection to or an affiliation with something.
From Latin associātiō, from associō (perhaps via French association). Morphologically associate + -ion.
To interact with others, especially personally, informally and off the clock rather than formally and officially.
From Latin dissociō + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dis- (“apart”) + sociō (“join”), from socius (“related, leagued”).
From Middle English upset (“the act of setting up; establishment”), from Middle English upsetten, corresponding to up- + set.
An additional piece of information, an addition to existing information.
From up- + date. First use appears c. 1948. (see Citations).
From Middle English upright, uppryght, upriht, from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”)
Located on a higher floor or level of a building.
To end up; to set on end.
Having a fast pace, tempo, or beat.
To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.
From Middle English upholden, equivalent to up- + hold.
The area in the interior of a country with a generally higher elevation.
From Middle English upland, from Old English ūpland (“the country”); equivalent to up- + land.
To raise something or someone to a higher physical, social, moral, intellectual, spiritual, or emotional level.
To tear up (a plant, etc.) by the roots, or as if by the roots; to extirpate, to root up.
From up- (prefix indicating a higher direction or position) + root (“to tear up by the roots; (figuratively) to remove forcibly from a place; to eradicate, exterminate”, verb). Root is derived…
The final result, or outcome of something.
From Middle English uptaken (“to take up, lift”), partial calque of earlier Middle English upnimen (“to take up, lift”), equivalent to up- + take.
An upward turn or trend, especially in business activity or profit.
From Middle English upturnen, equivalent to up- + turn.
From Middle English upbreiden, from Old English upbreġdan, equivalent to up- + braid.
From up- + chuck, from chuck up.
an upward current of air, especially a strong one
Toward or at the rear of a theatrical stage.
From up- + stage. The figurative uses “haughty” and “to draw attention away” derive from actors moving to a higher and thus more visible position on a sloped stage.
One who has suddenly gained wealth, power, or other prominence, but either has not received social acceptance or has become arrogant or presumptuous.
From Middle English upstarten, upsterten, equivalent to up- + start.
The cardinal number occurring after fourteen (14) and before sixteen (16).
From Middle English fiftene, from Old English fīftīene, fīftēne.
The cardinal number occurring after fifteen and before seventeen, represented in Arabic numerals as 16 and in Roman numerals as XVI.
Inherited from Middle English sextene, sixtene, from Old English sixtīene.
The cardinal number occurring after seventeen and before nineteen, represented in Roman numerals as XVIII and in Arabic numerals as 18.
From Middle English eightetene, eiȝtene, ehtetene, from Old English eahtatīene, eahtatēne.
The cardinal number occurring after thirteen and before fifteen.
From Middle English fourtene, from Old English fēowertīene.
The cardinal number occurring after eighteen and before twenty, represented in Roman numerals as XIX and in Arabic numerals as 19. It is the last/largest of the "teens".
From Middle English nyntene, nynetene, from Old English niġontīene, niġontēne.
The cardinal number occurring after twelve and before fourteen: ten and three.
From Middle English thirttene, variant (through metathesis) of thrittene, from Old English þrēotīene.
The cardinal number occurring after sixteen and before eighteen, represented in Roman numerals as XVII and in Arabic numerals as 17.
Inherited from Middle English seventene, from Old English seofontīene.
From Middle English toward, from Old English tōweard.
In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place; in a course toward the source or origin.
From Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -ward.
Situated toward or at the front of something.
From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“forward, inclined to the front, fore, early, former”)
From Middle English bakwarde, abakward, equivalent to back (adverb) + -ward.
Situated on the inside; that is within, inner; belonging to the inside.
From Middle English inward, from Old English inweard, corresponding to in + -ward.
On the side sheltered from the wind; in that direction.
From lee (“side away from the wind”) + -ward (“direction”).
From Middle English outward, from Old English ūtweard, equivalent to out + -ward.
Being in or facing towards the sea.
From Middle English seaward, seward (attested only as an adjective), equivalent to sea + -ward.
Given to a wilful, perverse deviation from the expected norm; tending to stray.
Toward a lower level, whether in physical space, in a hierarchy, or in amount or value.
The direction or area lying to the east.
From Middle English estward, from Old English ēastweard, ēasteweard; equivalent to east + -ward.
From Middle English homward, from Old English hāmweard.
Located, facing or moving in the direction of the land, as opposed to the sea.
The part that comes last or is situated in the rear; conclusion, wind-up.
Towards the wind, or the direction from which the wind is blowing.
With discomfort or lack of coordination.
Towards or in the direction of the Earth.
From Middle English ertheward, erþewarde, equivalent to earth + -ward.
A representation of a number composed of such symbols.
Of or relating to numbers, especially the characters 0 to 9.
From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”).
From Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). By surface analysis, Latin numerus + -ate.
Consisting of, or limited to, letters and/or numbers, especially the characters A to Z (lowercase and uppercase) and 0 to 9.
A person who works in a group, association, or public office without forming part of the regular staff (the numerary).
From Late Latin supernumerarius (“extra soldier added to a legion; supernumerary”)
Equally distant from one another at all points.
From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek παράνοια (paránoia, “madness”), from παράνοος (paránoos, “demented”), from παρά (pará, “beyond, beside”) + νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”).
A value kept constant during an experiment, equation, calculation, or similar, but varied over other versions of the experiment, equation, calculation, etc.
From French paramètre, from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).
A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase.
A small light umbrella used as protection from the sun.
From French parasol, from Italian parasole, from para- (“to shield”) + sole (“sun”).
An apparent shift in the position of two stationary objects relative to each other as viewed by an observer, due to a change in observer position.
From Middle French parallaxe, from Ancient Greek παράλλαξις (parállaxis, “alteration”) from παραλλάσσω (parallássō, “to cause to alternate”) from ἀλλάσσω (allássō, “to alter”) from ἄλλος (állos,…
Chiefly followed by of: a sudden outburst of violent activity or feeling; also, the most severe part of an activity or incident; the climax.
From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”)
Any of various mushrooms with broad, domed caps.
Borrowed from French parachute, from para- (“protection against”) (as in parasol) and chute (“fall”).
A state of being unable to act.
Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”). By surface analysis, para- + -lysis.
A person who is licensed at the state or national level to practice medical interventions in an emergency prehospital setting.
Of events, experiences, or phenomena, that cannot be explained by current scientific understanding or natural laws.
From para- (“beyond”) + normal; compare supernatural. First use appears c. 1905.
Of or relating to the provision of emergency medical treatment
A group of civilians trained and organized in a military fashion, but which do not represent the formal forces of a sovereign power.
A member of a parliament, congress or an elected national legislative body of another name.
A person who is trained to assist a professional: for example, an assistant to an educator.
To change with time or a similar parameter.
From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (“different, various”); see various.
From Middle French varieté (“variety”) (modern French variété (“variety; genre, type”)) or directly from its etymon Latin varietās (“difference; diversity, variety”) + English -ty (suffix forming…
More than one (of an indeterminate set of things).
Borrowed from Middle French varieux, from Latin varius (“manifold, diverse, various, parti-colored, variegated, also changing, changeable, fickle, etc.”). By surface analysis, vary + -ous.
Able to vary or be varied.
Borrowed into Middle English in the 14th century from Old French variable, from Latin variare (“to change”), from varius (“different, various”). Equates to English vary + -able.
From Late Latin variegāre (“to make of various sorts or colors”), from Latin varius (“various”) + agere (“to make, do”).
Streaked, spotted, or otherwise marked with a variety of color.
An element of personal character that enables one to distinguish the wise from the unwise.
From Middle English wisdom, from Old English wīsdōm (“wisdom”)
The lack of a specific constraint, or of constraints in general
From Middle English fredom, freedom, from Old English frēodōm (“freedom, state of free-will, charter, emancipation, deliverance”)
A realm, region, or conceptual space where something is dominant.
From Middle English kingdom, kyngdom, from Old English cyningdōm.
The fans of a sport, activity, work, person etc., taken as a group.
The death or suffering on account of adherence to the Christian faith, or to any cause.
From Middle English martyrdome, martirdom, marterdom, from Old English martyrdōm (“martyrdom”), corresponding to martyr + -dom.
The people elected to government or employed in the civil service.

meaning: The state or time of being
words: The state of being a child.
From Middle English childhode, childhod, from Old English ċildhād (“childhood”). By surface analysis, child + -hood.
The probability of a specified outcome; the chance of something happening; probability; the state or degree of being probable.
From Middle English liklihode, equivalent to likely + -hood.
The residential area near one's home.
From an alteration of earlier neighborred (“neighborhood”)
The state or condition of being a boy.
The state or condition of being a human being.
From Middle English manhode, also manhede (> obsolete English manhead), equivalent to man + -hood.
The state or period of infancy.
The state or condition of being a girl.
The state or condition, for humans and other animals, of physical and psychological maturity: being an adult.
From Middle English falshede, from false + -hede, equivalent to false + -hood.
The state of being a saint.
The property of being a state, an autonomous subdivision of a federal country.
The state or period of being a widow or widower.
From Middle English widwehede, equivalent to widow + -hood.
The state or condition of being a woman.
From Middle English womanhoode, wommanhod, whomanhode, variants of wommanhede. By surface analysis, woman + -hood.
The state of being a father (biological father, stepfather, adoptive father, foster father; sometimes the biological father specifically).
From Middle English faderhode, fadirhode, fadirhede, equivalent to father + -hood.
An honour whereby one is made into a knight, and whereafter one is entitled to be called Sir.
From Middle English knyghthode, knyȝthod, from Old English cnihthād.
A means of providing the necessities of life for oneself (for example, a job or income).
From Middle English liflode, from Old English līflād (“course of life, conduct”), from līf (“life”) + lād (“course, journey”), later altered under the influence of lively, -hood.
The condition of being a maiden; the time when one is a maiden or young girl.
From Middle English maydenhede, maydenhode, from Old English mæġdenhād (“maidenhood”). By surface analysis, maiden + -hood.
The state of being a mother.
From Middle English moderhode, moderhede, equivalent to mother + -hood.
The state of being a parent.
The role or office of a priest.
From Middle English presthed, presthede, presthod, presthode, from Old English prēosthād (“priesthood”), equivalent to priest + -hood.
Lacking good sense or judgement as a general trait; unwise; stupid.
From Middle English folisch; equivalent to fool + -ish.
Having excessive or exclusive regard and concern for one's own well-being, profit or pleasure, with little or no consideration for others.
From Middle English childisch, from Old English ċildisċ. By surface analysis, child + -ish.
Having a tint or hue similar to the colour blue.
From Middle English blewissh, blewisch (also Middle English bloysh), equivalent to blue + -ish.
Like a stereotypical boy in appearance or demeanor.
Mischievous; of or befitting an imp.
Characteristic of a mule; stubborn, obstinate, or intractable.
Characteristic of or resembling an oaf; clumsy, stupid.
Resembling or characteristic of an owl.
Dashingly, carelessly, or sportingly unconventional or stylish; jaunty; characterized by a devil-may-care unconventionality; having a somewhat disreputable quality or appearance.
From rake (“man habituated to immoral conduct”) + -ish.
Fond of reading or studying, especially said of someone lacking social skills as a result.
Characteristic of a cad, discourteous, ungentlemanly, dishonorable.
The state of a society being without authorities or an authoritative governing body.
From New Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía). By surface analysis, an- + -archy.
A short account of a real incident or person, often humorous or interesting.
Lacking a name; not named, for example an animal not assigned to any species .
Borrowed into English around 1600 from Late Latin anonymus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓νώνῠμος (ănṓnŭmos, “without name”)
From Middle English anodine, from Medieval Latin anōdynos (“stilling or relieving pain”), from Ancient Greek ἀνώδυνος (anṓdunos, “free from pain”), from ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ὀδύνη (odúnē, “pain”).
Without oxygen; especially of an environment or organism.
From French anaérobie, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic. By surface analysis, an- + aerobic.
A medication that performs this action: one that relieves pain.
Learned borrowing from New Latin analgēsia. By surface analysis, an- + algesia.
A drug used to reduce and manage pain, especially without inducing a loss of other sensation.
From analgesia (“absence of pain”) + -ic, from New Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἄλγησις (álgēsis, “sense of pain”), from ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
One who disregards laws and social norms as a form of rebellion against authority.
From French anarchiste, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía) from the roots ἀν- (an-, “without”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”), equivalent to anarchy + -ist.
A medication that provides the service of temporarily blocking sensation.
From an- + esthetic, or Latinized form of Ancient Greek ἀναίσθητος (anaísthētos, “insensible”) + -ic, from ἀν- (an-, “un-”) + αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós, “perceptible”).
To work or act together, especially for a common purpose or benefit.
From Medieval Latin coōrdinātus, perfect passive participle of coōrdinō (“arrange together”), from co- + ōrdinō, equivalent to co- + ordinate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.
Active help from a person, organization, etc., such as an orderly sharing of space or resources.
To restrain by force, especially by law or authority; to repress; to curb.
From Latin coërceō (“to surround, encompass, restrain, control, curb”), from co- (“together”) + arceō (“to inclose, confine, keep off”).
To sign a document jointly with another person, sometimes as an endorsement.
To feature (a number of star performers) jointly.
Equal to each other in size, rank or position.
From Middle English coequalle, from Latin coaequālis; equivalent to co- + equal.
To exist contemporaneously or in the same area.
Allied by blood; kindred by birth; specifically (law) related on the mother's side.
Borrowed from Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from co- + gnātus (“born”).
To live together with someone else, especially in a romantic and sexual relationship but without being married.
From Latin cohabitō; co- + habitō (“to dwell, to live in”).
A backup or assistant pilot of an aircraft.
Vast in quantity or number, profuse, abundant; taking place on a large scale.
From Middle English copious, from Latin copiosus, from copia (“abundance”), equivalent to co- + ops (“wealth”) + -osus (“full of”). By surface analysis, copy + -ous.
To join into a mass or whole.
From Latin coalēscō, from co- + alēscō (“grow up”).
An author who collaborates with another to write something.
Actual or threatened force for the purpose of compelling action by another person
