One who makes equal; a balancer.
Having two or more equally applicable meanings; capable of double or multiple interpretation.
From Late Latin aequivocus + -al, from aequus + vocō. By surface analysis, equi- + vocal.
The state of being calm, stable and composed, especially under stress.
From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. By surface analysis, equ- + anim(us) + -ity.
Occupying a position midway between two ends or sides.
From Middle French équidistant, from Late Latin aequidistantem, from aequī (“equal”) + distantem (“distant”). By surface analysis, equi- + distant.
A side exactly corresponding, or equal, to others.
The act of equalizing, or state of being equalized.
The use of expressions susceptible of a double signification, possibly intentionally and with the aim of misleading.

meaning: Of a generation removed from the original noun
words: The noun is derived from Middle English grandfadre, graundfadir, graunfadir, grauntfader, and other forms.
From Middle English graundmodre, grauntmoder, granmoder; equivalent to grand- + mother.
A familiar or disparaging term of address to an old man.
An electromagnetic wave with wavelength between that of infrared light and radio waves.
The entire CPU of a computer on a single integrated circuit (chip).
Borrowed from French microbe, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) and βίος (bíos, “life”). By surface analysis, micro- + -obe.
The collective microprograms in a CPU, used to run machine instructions.
Human nature or the human body as representative of the wider universe; man considered as a miniature counterpart of divine or universal nature.
From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”), equivalent to micro- + -cosm.
A continuous roll of film containing photographs of documents at a greatly reduced size.
A small loan, especially one extended to a poor person as part of a microcredit program of such lending intended to alleviate poverty.
A device used to magnify and read these sheets.
A device used to measure distance very precisely but within a limited range, especially depth, thickness, and diameter.
From French micromètre, equivalent to micro- + -meter.
A device (transducer) used to convert sound waves into a varying electric current; normally fed into an amplifier and either recorded or transmitted over radio.
An optical instrument used for observing small objects.
From New Latin microscopium and Italian microscopio, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”), equivalent to micro- + -scope.
An SI unit of time equal to 10⁻⁶ seconds. Symbol: μs
The branch of biology that deals with microorganisms, especially their effects on man and other living organisms.
Relating to techniques of surgery on very small or delicate parts of the body.
An organism that is too small to be seen by the unaided eye; especially, a single-celled organism, such as a bacterium.
The field of economics that deals with small-scale economic activities such as those of an individual or company.
Noon; twelve o'clock during the day.
From Middle English midday, from Old English middæġ (“midday, noon”), equivalent to mid- + day.
The middle of the night: the sixth temporal hour, equidistant between sunset and sunrise.
From Middle English midnight, from Old English midniht.
From Middle English mydwaye, mydweye, from Old English midweġ (“midway”), equivalent to mid- + way.
The region of a country not near the borders; the interior.
From Middle English mydlonde, equivalent to mid- + land.
The middle section of the human torso, from below the chest to above the waist; the abdomen and its back part.
From Middle English midref, mydrif, from Old English midrif, midhrif (“the midriff; diaphragm”)
Halfway through a term, or roughly so.
The part of a city between uptown and downtown.
The middle part of a year.
The middle of a stream or river.
The period around the summer solstice; around June 21st in the northern hemisphere.
From Middle English midsomer, midsumer, from Old English midsumer, midsumor (“midsummer”)
From Middle English midwinter, mydwinter, mydwynter, from Old English midwinter.
An exclusive control over the trade or production of a commodity or service through exclusive possession.
From Latin monopōlium, from Ancient Greek μονοπώλιον (monopṓlion, “a right of exclusive sale”), from μόνος (mónos, “sole”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”). By surface analysis, mono- + -poly.
A black and white image, especially such a photograph.
From Ancient Greek μονόχρωμος (monókhrōmos), from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”); mono- + -chrome.
A single lens, usually in a wire frame, and used to correct vision for only one eye.
One of the symbols used in either the I Ching divination or the Taixuanjing divination
From French monogramme, from the Classical Latin adjective monogrammus, from the conjectured Ancient Greek * μονόγραμμος (monógrammos, “outlined”, “drawn with single lines”).
Anything massive, uniform, and unmovable, especially a towering and impersonal cultural, political, or social organization or structure.
The noun is borrowed from French monolithe (“object made from a single block of stone”)
a railroad system where the trains run on one rail
Borrowed from French monorail, equivalent to mono- + rail.
Any oxide containing a single oxygen atom in each molecule or formula unit.
A scholarly book or a treatise on a single subject or a group of related subjects; especially, such a document that is written by one person.
A long, uninterrupted utterance that monopolizes a conversation.
Excessive interest or concentration on a singular object or subject.
The belief in a single deity (one god or goddess); especially within an organized religion.
Knowing or using a single language; written or spoken in a single language.
Borrowed from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, monosyllable + -ic or mono- + syllabic.
Believing in a single god, deity, spirit, etc., especially for an organized religion, faith, or creed.
Having only one color, represented by differing hues and tints. For example shades in a black and white television.
From mono- + chromatic, mono- from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”), chromatic from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).
A viral infection marked by extreme fatigue, high fever, and swollen lymph nodes.
A digital picture of any kind.
To fix permanently in the memory etc.
Of or pertaining to a lens system used to produce an enlarged image of a distant object.
A machine which reproduces documents by photographing the original over a glass plate and printing duplicates.
The art and technology of producing images on photosensitive surfaces, and its digital counterpart.
From French photographie. By surface analysis, photo- + -graphy, together meaning "drawing with light" or "representation by means of lines", "drawing". From φῶς (phôs, “of light”), and γράφω…
Of or relating to the electric effects of electromagnetic radiation, especially the ejection of an electron from a surface by a photon.
Having a reaction to, or able to be affected by, light.
Any process by which plants and other photoautotrophs convert light energy into chemical energy.
A form of journalism in which a story is told primarily through photographs and other images.
A large self-service store that sells groceries and, usually, medications, household goods, and/or clothing.
Above nature; beyond or added to nature, often so considered because it is given by a deity or some force beyond that with which humans are born.
From Middle English supernatural, supernaturel, from Middle French supernaturel, from Latin supernātūrālis, from super (“above”) + nātūra (“nature; that which we are born with”)
An übermensch; (loosely), a man of extraordinary powers.
A calque of German Übermensch; super- + man. The German word was introduced by the philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) in his work Also sprach Zarathustra (Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 1883),…
Something which is brilliant or explosive.
From super- (prefix meaning ‘exceptionally large in quantity, excessive; superior in potency or power’) + nova (“sudden brightening of a previously inconspicuous star”), coined by the German…
From Middle French superseder (“postpone, defer”), from Latin supersedēre.
To increase the size of something, especially to unusual proportions.
Someone who has accumulated a vast amount of fame; a high-level celebrity.
Beyond what is possible for a human being.
From Medieval Latin superhūmānus. By surface analysis, super- + human.
A highly paid, famous fashion model.
From super- + model. First written example dates from 1942 in the English language, in common use since the late 1980s. Sometimes incorrectly attributed to supermodel Janice Dickinson.
A sovereign state with dominant status on the globe and a very advanced military, especially the United States or formerly the Soviet Union.
Greater than the speed of sound (in the same medium, and at the same temperature and pressure).
To make faster or more powerful.
To place an object over another object, usually in such a way that both will be visible.
Placed above the normal line of text.
From Middle French superscript, from Latin superscriptus (“written above”). By surface analysis, super- + script.
An inlet air compressor for an internal combustion engine (either Otto or Diesel cycle).
An expressway, especially one designed for high speeds.
Retired or discarded due to age.
From the Latin superannuatus (“more than one year old”), from super (“over”) (English super-) + annus (“year”) (English annual).
The combined application of science and art in practical ways in industry, as for example in designing new machines.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología, “systematic treatment (of grammar)”), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art”) + -λογία (-logía, “study”). By surface analysis, techno- + -logy.
Of, relating to, or involving technology, especially modern scientific technology.
An expert in some technology, especially one in a managerial or administrative role.
Back-formation from technocracy, equivalent to techno- + -crat.
A system of governance where people who are skilled or proficient govern in their respective areas of expertise.
From techno- (“technical”, “technicians”) + -cracy (“rule by”), attributed to W.H. Smyth.
The use of living organisms (especially microorganisms) in industrial, agricultural, medical and other technological applications.
A set of three connected works—usually dramas, literary pieces, films, or musical compositions—all related by theme, characters, or setting.
Learned borrowing from Latin trilogia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τριλογία (trilogía, “trilogy”). Morphologically from tri- + -logy.
From Middle English triangle, from Old French triangle, from Latin triangulum, noun use of adjective triangulus (“three-cornered, having three angles”)
From Latin triad-, stem of trias (“three, triad”), from Ancient Greek τριάς (triás). By surface analysis, tri- + -ad.
Borrowed from Latin tripod- (stem of tripūs, tripodis), from Ancient Greek τρίποδ- (trípod-, stem of τρίπους, τρίποδος (trípous, trípodos), literally “three-footed”); equivalent to tri- + -pod.
A three-pronged spear somewhat resembling a pitchfork.
From Latin tridēns, from tri- (“three”) + dēns (“tooth”).
A cycle with three wheels, powered by pedals and usually intended for young children.
From French tricycle. By surface analysis, tri- + cycle.
A type of boat with three parallel hulls.
An athletics event in which contestants compete in swimming, cycling and running in turn.
From Latin triennium (“three-year period”), from tres (“three”) + annus (“year”). By surface analysis, tri- + -ennial.
Spectacles with corrective lenses that have three different powers per eye.
From tri- + focal (see focus). Coined by John Isaac Hawkins, their inventor, in 1826.
From Middle English triangulare, trianguler, triangulere, from Old French triangulaire, triangulier and Latin triangulāris. By surface analysis, tri- + -angular.
Borrowed from New Latin trilaterālis or from tri- + lateral.
Made thrice as much; threefold; tripled.
A lipid, an ester of glycerol and three fatty acids (the same or different); the major constituent of animal and vegetable fats.
Borrowed from Middle French uniforme, from Latin uniformis.
The sum of everything that exists in the cosmos.
From Middle English universe, from Old French univers.
The state of being in harmony or agreement; harmonious agreement or togetherness, synchronisation.
From Middle English unisoun, from Middle French unisson, from Medieval Latin ūnisonus (“having the same sound”), from ūni- + sonus (“sound”).
A pedal cycle that only has one wheel.
Of, or having, a single legislative chamber.
A modern creation (circa 1802), from New Latin ūnilaterālis (“one-sided”), from Latin ūnus (“one”) + laterālis (“sided, lateral”), equivalent to uni- + lateral.
Pertaining to only one direction, e.g.: where all component parts are aligned in the same direction in space.

meaning: A skill of a particular kind.
words: A vehicle capable of atmospheric flight due to interaction with the air, such as buoyancy or lift.
From Middle English handcrafte, handecraft, hond-craft, from Old English handcræft, equivalent to hand + -craft.
Any of the skills related to a woodland habitat, especially those relating to outdoor survival; these skills collectively.
A trade requiring skill of hand; manual occupation; handcraft.
A vehicle supported on a cushion of air, able to traverse many different types of terrain and travel over water, used for transport.
From hover + -craft. Originally a trademark by Saunders-Roe Limited, a British aero- and marine-engineering company.
A vehicle that travels through space.
Any vessel with implements designed to move it in arbitrary direction through one or various bodies of water: a boat, ship, sea scooter, or similar vehicle.
The practice of witches; magic, sorcery, or the use of supernatural powers to influence or predict events.
From Middle English wicchecraft, wicchecreft, from Old English wiċċecræft, equivalent to witch + -craft.

meaning: A participant in a specified form of government.
words: Constructed upon or in line with the principle of government chosen by the people.
From Middle French democratique (“pertaining to democracy, democratic”) (modern French démocratique), and its etymon Late Latin democraticus (“pertaining to democracy, democratic; democrat”)
An absolute ruler with infinite power.
Borrowed from French autocrate, itself from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”)
Someone who rules by virtue of his or her wealth.
From pluto- + -crat, after plutocracy, from Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth, riches”) + κράτος (krátos, “power, might”).
One of a ruling class; a noble (originally in Revolutionary France).
From French aristocrate (“aristocrat”), attested once in the 16th century but recoined in the Revolutionary era, from aristocratie (“aristocracy”), from Medieval Latin aristocratia.
A user on a wiki with the right to change users' access levels.
From French bureaucrate, equivalent to bureau + -crat.
An expert in some technology, especially one in a managerial or administrative role.
Back-formation from technocracy, equivalent to techno- + -crat.
A small flat case containing magnetic tape on two reels, used to record and play back audio and video material.
A small space within a dwelling, usually alongside a kitchen, used for informal dining; a dining alcove or nook.
Borrowed from Middle French rosette (in sense 15) and (modern) French rosette. By surface analysis, rose + -ette.
A clasp or clip for gathering and holding the hair.
Borrowed from French barrette, from barre (“a bar”) + -ette, literally a small bar.
A small, flexible, magnetic disk for storage and retrieval of data.
From disk + -ette, by analogy with cassette.
A small brick, typically made of charcoal and used for fuel.
From French briquette, from brique (“brick”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).
A minced, cooked food (usually meat or vegetables), which is deep-fried in fat and sometimes sprinkled with breadcrumbs.
Borrowed from French croquette, from croquer (“to crunch”) + -ette (suffix indicating diminution).
A short novel, synonymous with novella.
A type of soft, woven fabric, made to imitate flannel by raising or brushing the fibers in the weft. Frequently used in sleepwear, pillows, and bedding.
A small kitchen or area for preparing food, often just a part of a room.
A small diner or restaurant that serves lunch.
A cassette containing a blank or prerecorded videotape on which visual images and sounds are recorded for use with a VCR.

meaning: Something written, drawn or otherwise recorded.
words: A word or phrase that is created by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase.
One of the symbols used in either the I Ching divination or the Taixuanjing divination
From French monogramme, from the Classical Latin adjective monogrammus, from the conjectured Ancient Greek * μονόγραμμος (monógrammos, “outlined”, “drawn with single lines”).
A telegram transmitted via a submarine cable.
A graphical display of numerical data in the form of upright bars, with the area of each bar representing frequency.
Probably from Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “mast”) + γράμμα (grámma), although it is sometimes claimed to have been derived from historical + diagram; coined in 1891 by English mathematician Karl…
An X-ray picture of the breasts (mammaries), used to screen for breast cancer.
A small sheet of paper containing information, used for dissemination of said information, often an advertisement.
A band worn on the arm for ornamental or identification purposes.
A smooth-coated tablet (pill, as in medicine) shaped like a capsule, used as a tamper-resistant alternative to a capsule, or an easy-to-swallow alternative to regular tablets.
A thin slice of meat, usually fried.
From French côtelette (recorded in English since 1706), from Middle French costelette (“little rib”), from coste + -elette, from Old French coste (“rib, side”)
From Middle English oylet, from Old French oillet, equivalent to Old French oil (“eye”) + -et (diminutive suffix). Spelling and pronunciation were later on influenced by eye (which is distantly…
A young pig or swine, one not yet mature.
From pig + -let (diminutive suffix). Attested from 1855. Displaced Old English fearh.
A young actress with a promising career ahead of her.
From wave + -let; a calque of French ondelette, from onde (“wave”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).
A small colorless disk-shaped particle found in the blood of mammals, which plays an important role in the formation of blood clots.
Often used as an affectionate term of address: a person who is very dear to one.
The noun is derived from Middle English dereling, derelyng (“beloved person; beloved of God, devout Christian”), from Old English dīerling, dēorling (“favourite, darling; minion”)
From Late Middle English goslyng (“gosling”), alteration (due to Middle English goos (“goose”)) of earlier gesling (“gosling”), of North Germanic origin.
A young tree, larger than a seedling.
From Middle English saplyng, seplyng, sapling, equivalent to sap + -ling.
A person who shares a parent; one's brother or sister who one shares a parent with.
From Middle English dokeling, dukling, dookelynge (“duckling”), equivalent to duck + -ling.
A folk word, first attested in c. 1600s, apparently from a Norfolk (East Anglian) dialect, of uncertain origin.
From Middle English hirlyng, from Old English hȳrling (“hireling, employee”)
A small, young bird that is still confined to the nest.
From Middle English nestling, equivalent to nest + -ling.
A family, Sturnidae, of passerine birds.
From Middle English starling, sterling, sterlinge, from Old English stærling, from stær (“starling”) + -ling (diminutive suffix).
A young mammal not yet weaned and still being fed milk by its mother.
From Middle English sukling, sukeling, sokeling, equivalent to suck + -ling.
A person of weak or even sickly physical constitution.
An animal that is between one and two years old; one that is in its second year (but not yet two full years old).
From Middle English yerling, yerlyng, equivalent to year + -ling.
One who tills the earth; a farmer, a husbandman, a ploughman.
From Middle English erthling (“farmer, ploughman”) [and other forms] (in glossaries), from Old English ierþling, eorþling (“farmer, husbandman, ploughman”) [and other forms].
An abandoned child, left by its parent(s), often a baby left at a convent or similar safe place.
From Middle English foundlyng, fondeyng, variants of Middle English fyndling, fyndlyng. By surface analysis, found + -ling.
A seedling with most of the leaves stripped off.
From Middle English stripling (“an adolescent, a youth (specifically one who is male); a child”) [and other forms], possibly from strepen (“to remove the clothes of, undress, strip; to peel off;…
A subordinate, or person of lesser rank or authority.
From Middle English underling, from Old English underling. By surface analysis, under + -ling.
A person or object (especially when regarded as inferior) secretly exchanged for something else.
The noun is derived from change + -ling (suffix with the sense ‘immature; small’). Sense 6 (“idiot, simpleton”) is from the idea that foolish children had been left by magical creatures (sense 1).
Any straight line between two points on the circumference of a circle that passes through the center of the circle; a chord that passes through the center of the circle.
From Old French diametre (French diamètre), from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros) (γραμμή (grammḗ)) (diametros grammē, “line measuring across”)
A device that measures the magnitude of an electric current, especially one calibrated in amperes.
An instrument, usually embedded within the speedometer of a vehicle, that measures the distance the vehicle has traveled since production.
From French odomètre, from Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to odo- + -meter.
An instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure.
From baro- + -meter. Coined in 1665 by Robert Boyle as a name for the instrument invented by Torricelli some 20 years earlier; soon thereafter borrowed from English into various languages.
A device, often electronic, that measures the number of steps taken, and thus estimates the distance walked.
An instrument for measuring electric potential in volts.
An instrument for measuring and recording the speed of the wind, a windmeter.
An instrument that floats in a liquid and measures its specific gravity on a scale.
An instrument that measures the humidity of the air or other gases, especially the relative humidity.
A device used to measure distance very precisely but within a limited range, especially depth, thickness, and diameter.
From French micromètre, equivalent to micro- + -meter.
A device for measuring the revolutions per minute (RPMs) of a revolving shaft, as with the driveshaft of an automobile.
A device for measuring time, particularly a precision mechanism for measuring time of day.
From chrono- + -meter, possibly after the model of earlier French chronomètre (“metronome”), ultimately from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + μέτρον (métron, “meter, measuring device”).
An instrument located within the dashboard of a vehicle that measures and indicates the current speed of the vehicle.
From speed + -o- + -meter; by surface analysis, speed + -ometer.
An apparatus used to measure temperature.
Borrowed from French thermomètre; equivalent to thermo- + -meter.
A device used to indicate the presence and direction of a small electric current, especially used to detect a null or balanced condition in a bridge circuit.
A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.
Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”)
Identification with or understanding of the thoughts, feelings, or emotional state of another person.
A 20th-century borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμπάθεια (empátheia, literally “passion”) (formed from ἐν (en, “in, at”) + πάθος (páthos, “feeling”)), equivalent to em- + -pathy, coined by Edward…
An agent that can cause disease, especially an infectious microorganism, such as a bacterium, virus, protozoon or fungus.
Natural contrariety or incompatibility between things, as a result of which they negatively affect or oppose each other; (countable) an instance of this.
Borrowed from Middle French antipathie (“deep dislike; object of dislike; incompatibility between things”) (modern French antipathie (“dislike, antipathy”)), and from its etymon Latin antipathīa…
Pathosis: any deviation from a healthy or normal structure or function; abnormality; illness or malformation.
From French pathologie, from Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “disease”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”). By surface analysis, path- + -ology or patho- + -logy.
A system of treating diseases with small amounts of substances which, in larger amounts, would produce the observed symptoms.
From German Homöopathie, equivalent to English homeo- + -pathy.
The branch of therapy based on manipulation of bones and muscles.
A specialist who examines samples of body tissues for diagnostic or forensic purpose.

meaning: Instrument used for viewing or examination.
words: A monocular optical instrument that magnifies distant objects, especially in astronomy.
The position of the planets and stars at the moment of someone's birth; a diagram of such positions.
Borrowed from Middle French horoscope, from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos)
A form of viewing device that allows the viewer to see things at a different height level and usually with minimal visibility.
An optical instrument used for observing small objects.
From New Latin microscopium and Italian microscopio, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”), equivalent to micro- + -scope.
Capable of seeing distant objects; far-seeing.
A device used to view continuous live X-ray images on a fluorescent screen.
From fluoro- + -scope, originally after German Fluorescop.
A medical instrument used for listening to sounds produced within the body.
Borrowed from French stéthoscope, a word coined by its inventor, physician René Laennec, equivalent to stetho- + -scope.
A constantly changing series of colours or other things.
The noun is derived from Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, “beautiful, lovely”) + εἶδος (eîdos, “form, image, shape”) + English -scope (suffix denoting an instrument used for examination or viewing),…
An electronic measuring instrument that creates a visible two-dimensional graph, on a screen, of one or more continuously varying voltages or currents.
An optical instrument used for spectrographic analysis .
The use of spectrometers in chemical analysis.
An area located outside of towns and cities; an area that is not urban or suburban; a rural area.
A position at the side of one's bed.
From Middle English bedsyde, bedde syde (also as beddes side, beddes syde), equivalent to bed + -side.
Beside the ring, especially a boxing ring.
The land bordering a body of water.
From Middle English water-syde, water side, equivalent to water + -side.
The part of the day from noon or lunchtime until sunset, evening, or suppertime or 6pm.
From Middle English afternone, after-non, equivalent to after- + noon.
Childcare services tending to children after the school day.
The glow seen in the sky after sunset.
A conscious existence after death; a supernatural life that follows one's natural life, in some worldviews.
That which happens after, that which follows, usually of strongly negative connotation in most contexts, implying a preceding catastrophe.
a lotion, gel, or liquid used after finishing shaving
By extension, any result or consequence following a major event.
A taste of something that persists when it is no longer present.
A device in a jet engine which injects fuel into the exhaust system to increase the thrust.
Any delayed effect; an effect which is not immediately manifested.
A reflection after an act; a later or subsequent thought, action, or expedient.
From after- + thought, probably modelled on forethought.
As if played with a scythe.
Of, or relating to, the ownership, tenure and cultivation of land.
From Middle French agrarien, from Latin agrarius (“of the land”), from stem of ager (“field”) + -arius.
The science of utilizing plants, animals and soils for food, fuel, feed, fiber, etc.
From French agronomie, from agronome (“agriculturist”), from Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós, “field”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). By surface analysis, agro- + -nomy.
The art or science of cultivating the ground, including the growing and harvesting of crops, and the rearing and management of livestock.
From Middle English agriculture, partly from Middle French agriculture and partly from its etymon Latin agricultūra, from ager (“field”) + cultūra (“cultivation”). See acre and culture.
Business (especially big business) connected to agriculture, either owning or operating large-scale farms, or catering to those who do.
From agri- + business, or a blend of agriculture + business, coined by American academic and diplomat John Herbert Davis (1904–1988).
A farmer; one involved with agrarian business.
Unwilling or unable to cooperate and associate normally with other people.
An agent that counteracts or neutralizes acidity, especially in the stomach.
A substance that induces an immune response, usually foreign (nonself) but not always so.
From French antigène, from anti- + gène.
A protein produced by B-lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen.
From anti- + body, a calque of German Antikörper.
A protagonist who proceeds in an unheroic manner, such as by criminal means, via cowardly actions, or for mercenary goals.
Of an additive added to petroleum/gasoline to reduce the occurrence of engine knock.
Natural contrariety or incompatibility between things, as a result of which they negatively affect or oppose each other; (countable) an instance of this.
Borrowed from Middle French antipathie (“deep dislike; object of dislike; incompatibility between things”) (modern French antipathie (“dislike, antipathy”)), and from its etymon Latin antipathīa…
A medicine able to neutralize a toxin.
Opposed to or against the establishment or existence of trusts (monopolies), usually referring to legislation.
Inhibiting the growth and reproduction of a virus.
A piece of software that is used to detect, delete and or neutralize computer-based viruses.
To work against; to oppose (especially to incite a reaction).

Opposed to the practice of slavery.

From Latin circumscrībō, from circum (“around”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, circum- + scribe.

Borrowed from Latin circumnāvigātus, perfect passive participle of circumnāvigō (“sail round something, circumnavigate”), from circum (“about, around”) + nāvigō (“sail, navigate”)
Attention to all the facts and circumstances of a case; consideration of all that is pertinent.

From Latin circumstantia + English -al, equivalent to circumstance + -ial.
The act of circumscribing or the quality of being circumscribed.
The study of the physical universe, its structure, dynamics, origin and evolution, and fate.
From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”), combination form of -λόγος (-lógos, “one who speaks (in a certain manner)”). By…

An astronaut, especially a Russian or Soviet one.
Borrowed from Russian космона́вт (kosmonávt), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “universe”) + ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”). By surface analysis, cosmo- + -naut.
From Middle French macrocosme (from Old French macrocosme) and Medieval Latin macrocosmus, formed from Ancient Greek μακρός (makrós, “great, long”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”).

An adult male singer who uses head tone or falsetto to sing far higher than the typical male vocal range.
From Latin contrātenor. By surface analysis, counter- + tenor.

A weight that is put in opposition to an equal weight so it keeps that in balance.

A solid figure with many flat faces and straight edges.
From New Latin polyedron, from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”)
Able to play more than one musical note at the same time.

The belief in the existence of multiple gods.
From French polythéisme, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) and θεός (theós, “god”), corresponding to poly- + theism.
Having or relating to the ability to take multiple data types for a single parameter.
A vinylic polymer of styrene, CH₂CHphenyl.

Like a living being; resembling life; being an accurate representation.

Like something from a dream; having a sense of vagueness, insubstantiality, or incongruousness.
Befitting or characteristic of a woman.
Resembling or characteristic of a workman.
Methodical and efficient, in a way that would be advantageous to a business or businessperson.
Demonstrating good sportsmanship, behaving in an honorable and appropriate manner.
Like a statesman, demonstrating the skills and qualities of a respected leader.
Violating the accepted standards of sportsmanship.
From Middle English utmost, utemest [and other forms], from Old English ūtmest, ūtemest [and other forms].
At or nearest to the top; uppermost; being the very highest.
From Middle English innermost, innermest, in-nermast, alteration (due to Middle English inner, innere (“inner”)) of Old English innemest (“innermost”), equivalent to inner + -most.
In the lowest position or state; bottom.
superlative form of upper: most upper.
From Middle English upper-moste; equivalent to upper + -most.

meaning: Forms nouns meaning voyager or traveller
words: Of, relating to, or characteristic of sailing, sailors, or the sea.
From Middle French nautique (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) or its etymon, Classical Latin nauticus (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), + -al (adjectival suffix). Nauticus is from…
A member of the crew of a spaceship or other spacecraft that travels beyond Earth's atmosphere, or someone trained to serve that purpose.
From astro- + -naut. Coined from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) and ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”).
An astronaut, especially a Russian or Soviet one.
Borrowed from Russian космона́вт (kosmonávt), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “universe”) + ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”). By surface analysis, cosmo- + -naut.
A literal or metaphorical force or object regarded as unstoppable, that will crush all in its path.
Borrowed in the 17th century into British English in India, either through Hindustani جَگَنَّاتھ (jagannāth) / जगन्नाथ (jagannāth) or directly from Odia ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ (jagannātha), ultimately from…
Of or pertaining to the scientific study of flight
From French astronautique (“astronautics”) + English -ics. By surface analysis, astro- (“space”) + nautics (“navigation”).

meaning: Resembling; having the likeness of (usually including the concept of not being the same despite the likeness, but counterexamples exist).
words: Of or relating to lymphatic glands or lymphoid tissue.
A robot that is designed to look and act like a human being (not necessarily a male one).
Learned borrowing from New Latin androīdēs, from Ancient Greek ἀνδροειδής (androeidḗs, “human-shaped”). By surface analysis, andr- + -oid.
From French colloïde, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”) + -oid.
Being the process of the temporal bone behind the ear.
Borrowed from New Latin mastoīdēs, from Ancient Greek μᾰστοειδής (măstoeidḗs, “like a breast”), from μᾰστός (măstós, “a woman's breast”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).
A compact or compressed version of something; especially something having a popular or sensational nature.
The noun is derived from tabl(et) + -oid (suffix meaning ‘having the likeness of, resembling’), originally coined by the United Kingdom firm Burroughs, Wellcome & Company as a brand name for their…
Any of many organic (often heterocyclic) bases that occur in nature and often have medicinal properties.
A naturally occurring solid object, which is smaller than a planet and a dwarf planet, larger than a meteoroid and not a comet, that orbits a star and often has an irregular shape.
Being anthropomorphic under some criteria (physical, mental, genetical, ethological, ethical etc.).
From human (from Latin hūmānus m (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”, adjective)) + -oid.
A coil of wire that acts as a magnet when an electric current flows through it.
From French solénoïde, from Ancient Greek σωληνοειδής (sōlēnoeidḗs) (from σωλήν (sōlḗn, “channel, pipe”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs); see -oid).
A solid of revolution generated by rotating an ellipse about its major (prolate), or minor (oblate) axis.
Having characteristics of a human, usually in terms of shape or appearance.
From Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποειδής (anthrōpoeidḗs). By surface analysis, anthrop- + -oid.
Of a device: protected against, or designed to be proof against, misuse or error.
Resistant to rust, oxidation and corrosion.
Designed to be unable for a child to use, operate, or open.
Made sturdily enough to withstand knocks and shocks without being damaged.
Resistant to the effects of water.
Capable of withstanding a direct shot by a bullet fired from a gun.
Resistant to shattering; difficult to break.
Capable of resisting damage caused by the weather.
Someone who acts in a disreputable, unethical, or unscrupulous way, especially in the practice of law and politics.
A member of a criminal or street gang.
A peddler or hawker, who sells small items, either door-to-door, from a stall, or in the street.

From Middle English hukster, probably of Low German or Dutch origin, from Middle Low German höken (“to peddle”) or Middle Dutch hokester, itself from hoeken (“to peddle, bend, bear on the back”), all.
A person who lives along the road.
From Middle English songster, sangester, sangstere, from Old English sangestre (“a female singer; songstress”), equivalent to song + -ster.
A spin doctor, spin merchant or spinmeister.
From Middle English spynnestere (“woman who spins fibre”)
A singer in a choir; especially a child in a church or cathedral choir.
Derived from late Middle English queristre, from an Anglo-Norman variant of Old French cueriste, from cuer (see Middle French cuer). Equivalent to choir + -ster.
One who is noted for being very fast.
From young + -ster. Attested from the early 17th century.
Accesories or clothing that is worn on the foot; a shoe, sandal, etc.
Men's clothing (and accessories), particularly in a retail context.
garments designed to be worn in bed; nightclothes
Clothes worn next to the skin, underneath outer clothing.
Casual clothing that is comfortable to wear when exercising or partaking in sport; activewear.
A painting, drawing, sculpture or other piece of creative, visual art.
Ornamental woodwork either carved in low relief or cut through.
Anything made wholly or largely of iron, especially when used for decoration.
From Middle English ironwerk, irynwerk, equivalent to iron + -work.
The action of behaving mechanically in the manner of a clock.
From Middle English stonewerk, stonwerk, ston-werke, stoonwerk, from Old English stānweorc; equivalent to stone + -work.
The construction or repair of bridges.
The art or process of working with a needle especially in embroidery or needlepoint.
A thing or things made of wicker.
A lattice or lattice-like structure; interlacing laths or strips.

meaning: Of sufficient worth for; deserving of.
words: Interesting enough to be reported as a news
Deserving attention; notable; worthy of notice.
Being able to be driven, or suitable for driving, on the open road.
From Middle English blame worthy, blame-worthy, equivalent to blame + -worthy.
Meriting praise; worthy of high praise
A mixture of fine solid particles or liquid droplets suspended in a gaseous medium.
The atmosphere of the Earth and the region of space around it.
Having a shape that reduces drag when moving through the air.
The design, construction, mathematics, and mechanics of aircraft and other flying objects; the study of and control of how aviation works.
Borrowed from French aéronautique or New Latin aeronauticus. By surface analysis, aero- + nautic + -s.
The science of the dynamics of bodies moving relative to gases, especially the interaction of moving objects with the atmosphere.
Of or pertaining to the scientific study of flight
In an aerodynamic manner, in a manner which reduces drag.
Relating to water; living in or near water, taking place in water.
Borrowed from Middle French aquatique (“living in water”), from Latin aquaticus (“relating to water”), from aqua (“water”).
A tank, often made of glass, for keeping live fish or other aquatic animals.
Borrowed from Latin aquārium, neuter of aquārius (“of or pertaining to water”), from aqua + -arium.
An artificial channel that is constructed to convey water from one location to another.
A board on which a person stands to ride for leisure which is pulled on a water surface by a motorboat.
The noun is derived from aqua- (prefix meaning ‘water’) + plane (“flat or level surface”) (ultimately.
The bluish-green colour of the sea.
From Latin aqua marīna (“sea water”), adjective form from mare (“sea”).
The cultivation of aquatic produce such as aquatic plants, fish, and other aquatic animals.
Being problematic over an extended period of time.
From chronical, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). By surface analysis, chron- + -ic.
A written account of events and when they happened, ordered by time.
From Middle English cronicle, cronycle, from Anglo-Norman cronicle, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of or concerning time”)
The science of determining the order in which events occurred.
From chrono- (“relating to time”) + -logy (“study of, account of”), after New Latin chronologia from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + λόγος (lógos, “reason, explanation”). Literally "time…
A chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object.
From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”)
In a chronic manner, or to a chronic degree.
A device for measuring time, particularly a precision mechanism for measuring time of day.
From chrono- + -meter, possibly after the model of earlier French chronomètre (“metronome”), ultimately from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + μέτρον (métron, “meter, measuring device”).
To cause two or more events or actions to happen at exactly the same time or same rate, or in a time-coordinated way.
From Ancient Greek συγχρονίζω (sunkhronízō), equivalent to syn- + chrono- + -ize.
At the same time, at the same frequency.
Borrowed from Late Latin synchronus, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos, “contemporaneous”)
Erroneous in date; in a wrong time; not applicable to or not appropriate for the time.
Relating to time, or units of time.
The state or property of being synchronized.

meaning: Shaped like a cross or X; crossing lines.
words: To mark with a pattern of transverse bars.
From Middle English crose bar, equivalent to cross- + bar.
Produced by breeding from two breeds, varieties or species.
The danger to a third party passing between two belligerents firing at one another.
Extending across a city or town.
To produce (an organism) by the mating of individuals of different breeds, varieties, or species; hybridize.
A horizontal or transverse beam or similar member that extends across or perpendicular to something.
An inscription on a gravestone in memory of the deceased.
From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”)
A term used to characterize a person or thing.
From Middle French épithète, from Latin epithetum, epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton, “epithet, adjective”), the neuter of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “additional”)
The embodiment or encapsulation of a class of items.
From Middle French, from Latin epitomē, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτομή (epitomḗ, “an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from ἐπιτέμνω (epitémnō, “to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”)
A widespread disease that affects many humans in a population.
From French épidémique, from épidémie, from Medieval Latin epidēmia, reanalysis of plural Late Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios)
A short speech, spoken directly at the audience at the end of a play
Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”)
The outer, protective layer of the skin of vertebrates.
Borrowed from Latin epidermis, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”). Equivalent to epi- + dermis.
Digital text in which the reader may navigate related information through embedded hyperlinks.
From hyper- + text; coined by American information technologist, philosopher, and sociologist Ted Nelson in 1965.
An n-dimensional Euclidian space with n > 3.
Having an increased state of activity
A shop combining elements of a department store and a supermarket.
From hyper- + market, calque of French hypermarché.
A state of great (nervous or emotional) tension.
Excessive and pathological movement and restlessness.
Highly or abnormally sensitive to some substances or agents, especially to some allergen.
To breathe quickly and deeply, especially at an abnormally rapid rate.
Any heightened immune response to an antigen; an allergy; hypersensation.
The state of breathing faster or deeper than necessary.

meaning: Smaller version of an item than usual.
words: A small bus, especially one used as transport for small groups.
From mini- + bus. In the political sense, probably a back-formation from omnibus.
A small van, especially (Canada, US, Australia, New Zealand, Philippines) one primarily used for family transport.
From mini- + van. First widely used in the 1980s, when this class of vehicles became widely popular as an alternative to station wagons (estate cars). Attested earlier in technical usage, usually…
A small motorized two-wheeled vehicle, just big enough for one adult to ride; such bikes are rarely street-legal.
Greatly diminished size or form; reduced scale.
Borrowed from Italian miniatura (“manuscript illumination”), from miniare (“to illuminate”), from Latin miniō (“to colour red”)
A short skirt with its hemline well above the knees, generally at mid-thigh level.
A radio or television series with a small number of episodes not intended to last a complete season.
To physically shrink in size, i.e. through the use of a shrink ray.
A computer smaller than a mainframe, but larger than a microcomputer.
The act or process of miniaturizing or making smaller.

meaning: More than one; pertaining to more than one thing.
words: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.
From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”),…
The combined use of sound, video, and text to present an idea.
The world, considered as lacking in purpose, design, or predictability.
Requiring or allowing multiple (or more than the usual two) players to play simultaneously.
A device that interleaves several activities; a switching device.
Composed of, or having a mixture of, multiple races.
Of, relating to, or involving multiple languages.
Designed or intended to fit more than one type of function or application; having multiple uses.
Having, involving, or relating to multiple variables.
Containing or relating to multiple vitamins.
Relating or pertaining to several different cultures.
Of, or involving more than two nations (externally between countries or internally in a country).
Computation using more than one processor.
A person whose net worth is multiple million dollars, pounds, euros or some other currency.
An anthology of previously released material linked together by theme or author, especially in book form.
Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus (“(carriage) for all”), from Latin omnibus (“for all”), dative plural of omnis (“all”).
An animal which is able to consume both plants (like a herbivore) and meat (like a carnivore).
From the Latin omnivorus. By surface analysis, omni- + -vore.
From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).
Having a diet which is neither exclusively carnivorous nor exclusively herbivorous.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.
From Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from Latin omni- (“all”), and scient from the Latin scientia (“knowledge”).
The ability to be, or the characteristic of being, at all places at the same time (usually only attributed to God).
The beginning of a musical note or other sound, in which the amplitude rises from zero to an initial peak.
A forceful rush or flow forward.
From Middle English on comynge, oncomynge, oncoomynge; equivalent to on- + coming (noun).
One who looks on or watches, without becoming involved or participating; an observer, a spectator.
From on- (prefix meaning ‘at; on, upon’) + looker (“one that looks”), from the verb look on.
From on- + slaught. Formed after Middle Dutch aenslag, aenslach, equivalent to aen + slag, although slaught corresponds to Middle Dutch slacht; slag is cognate with the English weaving term sley.
To supply (a device, structure, etc.) with new components or parts that were not previously available or installed; to modernize.
The verb is derived from retro- (prefix meaning ‘back; backward’) + fit (“to equip, supply”).
Directed or moving backwards in relation to the normal or previous direction of travel; retreating.
The adjective is derived from Middle English retrograd, retrograde (“of a planet: appearing to move in a direction opposite to the order of the zodiac signs, retrograde; unfortunate”)
To return to an earlier, simpler or worse condition; to regress.
From Latin retrōgressus, perfect active participle of retrōgradior (“retrograde”).
Borrowed from Latin retrōspectum, from retrōspicio (“to look back at”), equivalent to retro- + -spect.
Extending in scope, effect, application or influence to a prior time or to prior conditions.
A small rocket engine on a larger rocket or spacecraft, designed to slow or reverse its motion.
Of, relating to, or contemplating the past.
From retrospect + -ive. From Latin retrōspectus, perfect passive participle of retrōspiciō (“to look back at”).
One of two parts, equal or unequal, in which a whole tone is divided.
A playoff in the round with only four players or teams left, the stage before the final.
From Latin semifinalis, equivalent to semi- + final.
A periodical published twice a week.
Occurring twice a month or at half month intervals.
Partially retired; working part time, or not yet receiving pension benefits nor drawing down retirement savings.
In the shape of half of a circle or a semicircle.
A substance with electrical properties intermediate between a good conductor and a good insulator.
Neither fully conscious nor unconscious, partially aware but confused or distracted.
Permeable to some things and not to others, as a cell membrane which allows some molecules through but blocks other substances.
Paid as a professional but on a part-time basis.
A bottle, flask or similar vessel having a vacuum between its inner and outer silvered walls; designed to maintain the temperature of its contents
A device that automatically responds to changes in temperature by activating a heating or cooling system to maintain the temperature at a desired setting.
An apparatus used to measure temperature.
Borrowed from French thermomètre; equivalent to thermo- + -meter.
having or maintaining a consistent temperature
Of, or relating to the conversion of heat into other forms of energy.
Of, or relating to the fusion of atomic nuclei at high temperatures.
Softening when heated and hardening when cooled, and thus able to be moulded, remelted, and remoulded.
The science of the conversions between heat and other forms of energy.
From thermo- + dynamics. First attested in the 1850s.
